content.thinking:
I'm drafting the postmortem and starting with the symptom: latency rose, so the slowest requests got much slower. The logs mention account pages, but the latency metric is service-wide p99, and I'm weighing whether to describe it to users as shoppers' pages loading far more slowly, since render_spend_summary on account pages isn't directly shown yet.

I'm laying out the causal chain now: the slowdown traces to requests taking the typical-spend path after the typical-purchase-feature flag was switched on at P1, and turning that flag off restored service. I'm also checking whether any deploys or other changes could explain it, and so far only the flag change appears.

I'm working out the causal chain now: requests started taking the typical-spend path once the typical-purchase-feature flag was switched on at P1, and I'm checking whether any deploys or other changes could account for it instead, which so far they don't.

I'm settling on the root cause: the typical-spend function finds the median by repeatedly removing the minimum, so its work grows with the square of a shopper's history, and long-history shoppers pay a large cost once the flag is on.

I'm settling on the cause in plain terms: switching on the feature moved shoppers' typical-spend calculation onto a method that gets much slower as a shopper's purchase history grows, so shoppers with long histories saw their pages take far longer. Next I'm thinking about what could recur, since the same slow method is still in place and turning the feature back on would bring the slowdown back.

I'm now weighing a contributing factor: no check appears to have measured the latency of the flagged path before the flag was turned on, and the flip went from off to fully on without a gradual rollout.

I'm weighing whether the fix for this should be a check that every change behind a flag gets a latency test with long-history accounts before it's switched on, plus rolling flags out gradually with a p99 guard. I'm also noting that paging wouldn't have shortened the outage, since Argus mitigated it quickly.

I'm weighing whether nobody being paged should go under what went wrong, since the alert fired but no on-call incident was linked, and I'm considering an action item to tie high-latency alerts on this service to on-call paging. I'm also thinking the missing test bounding the work of the typical-spend function on long histories is a safeguard gap worth recording as its own contributing factor, tied to the item that adds that test.

I'm listing the action items now: one to require a latency check on long-history accounts before a flag is switched on, one to ramp flag changes gradually, one to link the latency alert to on-call paging, and a follow-up on the quadratic spend calculation on the flag-off path.

I'm listing the postmortem's good points now: Argus turned the flag off, the investigator tied the slowdown to the flag change, and the mitigation was confirmed. I'm also noting that the code-fix agent proposed a draft fix, which I'll record without describing what it does.

I'm sorting out the remaining parts of the postmortem: the fact that nobody was paged is worth recording as its own finding, and I'm considering whether the slowdown affected only the slowest requests. I'm also noting that the claim about which shoppers were slowed comes from the code-fix reading, since per-shopper latency wasn't actually measured.

I'm drafting the step that describes the slowest requests taking far longer than usual while the failure count stayed level, without adding any figures yet.

I'm working through the steps of the causal chain: the slowest requests got much slower after the flag was switched on, and the new path calls the spend calculation for every shopper's summary.

action_items.item: Before any feature flag that enables a new code path is switched on in production, require a latency check of that path against accounts with long purchase histories.
Roll out io-shop feature flags to a small share of traffic first, and widen them only while slowest-request latency stays at baseline.
Link the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person.
Make average_spend_per_item in spend_summary.py, the flag-off path that Code-Fix read as also growing with the square of history length, scale to long histories, and add a test that bounds its work.

causal_chain.step: The slowest requests to io-shop took far longer than usual. Its slowest-request latency rose from the minute the incident began, and no more requests failed than before.

ruled_out.what: A deploy: none came back for the day before the onset.
Any other flag change: the flag provider's history showed only one flag change by anyone but Argus in the hour before it was read.

causal_chain.step: Requests started going through the flag-on path when admin switched typical-purchase-feature on at {P1.1}. Before that, the service's flag evaluations were all off (Ga6f5). They were split during {Gc8c4.6} (Gc8c4) and all on from then until the alert (Gd44a).
With the flag on, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item to build the shopper's spend summary.
Code-Fix read typical_spend_per_item's work as growing with the square of a shopper's purchase history, so requests for shoppers with long histories became slow.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a feature made the shop use a new way of working out a shopper's typical spend, and that method likely slows down sharply for shoppers with a long purchase history, so their pages took much longer to load.

contributing_factors.factor: Before typical-purchase-feature was switched on, no check was seen that measured the latency of the code path it enabled for shoppers with long purchase histories.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The slowdown on the flag-on path would have been found before production traffic took that path.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag was switched on for all traffic at once: evaluations went from all off to all on within a minute, with no gradual rollout seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Only a small share of requests would have taken the slow path at first, and the rise could have been caught and the flag turned off before it reached everyone.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that bounds how much work typical_spend_per_item does on a long purchase history.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The function's growth with history length would have been caught in testing before any flag sent requests to it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent formed a single candidate, C1, tying the onset to the switch of typical-purchase-feature.
The Mitigation Agent switched typical-purchase-feature off. The change can be undone.
The Mitigation Agent checked the service and confirmed that switching the flag off had brought it back from the incident's level.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix to typical_spend_per_item, with tests, as draft PR #545.

went_wrong: The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

input.root_cause: With use_typical_spend true, render_spend_summary calls typical_spend_per_item (src/io_shop/typical_spend.py). Code-Fix read that function as finding the middle price by repeatedly scanning the purchase history for its minimum and then scanning again to remove it, about half the history's length times over. That makes its work grow with the square of the history's length, so only requests for shoppers with long histories pay a large cost.
input.still_at_risk: Switching typical-purchase-feature back on, or sending any other request to the typical-spend calculation, could again make requests for shoppers with long purchase histories very slow.
input.symptom: The slowest io-shop requests took far longer to load
